## Evidence brief: sertraline during lactation

**Identity:** The tool matched sertraline exactly (RxNorm 36437). Evidence was retrieved for sertraline as a single ingredient; it does not establish safety for combination products or interactions. [RxNorm](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### 1. Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed includes reports of decreased milk supply after starting sertraline, including a small observation involving six patients; timing, dose details, and alternative explanations were limited. It also describes a small mixed-SSRI study in which lactogenesis was delayed, but later feeding difficulties did not differ statistically. These findings are not specific enough to establish that sertraline caused a change in milk production. [LactMed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed product lists adult adverse-reaction categories including bleeding risk, serotonin syndrome, hyponatremia, seizures, and other warnings. However, the retrieved label did not include standalone sections for warnings, boxed warning, warnings/precautions, or drug interactions; this is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that those sections are absent from the full label. [DailyMed—SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET, RemedyRepack Inc.](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- **Label selection caveat:** This is one product label, not all sertraline formulations. It was effective November 5, 2026, and DailyMed notes that in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. The returned warning was titled “8.2 Lactation” with code 42229-5, but the tool flagged a title/code mismatch requiring verification.

### 2. Measured infant exposure

- LactMed reports that sertraline is detectable in milk at varying concentrations and that norsertraline is often detectable at low levels in infant serum. In one PubMed study of 12 mothers and 11 mother–infant pairs, sertraline was detected in three infants and the metabolite in six; infant serum concentrations were below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. [PubMed PMID 9286185](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)
- The DailyMed label reports a pooled analysis of 53 mother–infant pairs in which exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels of 2% of maternal levels, with a reported range of 0%–15%. [DailyMed](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- Milk and infant-serum concentrations are **exposure measurements**, not administered doses and not treatment instructions. LactMed’s drug-level section was truncated in the returned extract, so some pharmacokinetic details are incomplete.

### 3. Observed infant outcomes

- LactMed reports no observed adverse effects in several small observational samples, including groups of infants with normal reported weight gain and no abnormal effects reported by mothers. These samples were small and heterogeneous, so they do not establish safety for every infant or lactation context. [LactMed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One case involved a preterm infant exposed during pregnancy and breastfeeding who developed hyperthermia, abnormal muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying; the infant also had elevated serum concentrations. The source attributed the reaction to sertraline in the context of prematurity and reduced metabolism. This is a single case report, and its chronology is only partially represented in the returned extract. [LactMed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Another report involved infant sedation where the mother was also taking other sedating medicines; attribution to sertraline alone is not established. [LactMed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed’s infant-effects section was truncated, including at least one later case passage, so the returned record is not complete. A longer retrieval would be needed to summarize the omitted chronology accurately.

### Literature context

The tool returned a bounded PubMed search of 129 records and abstracts for five relevance-ranked records, including the 1997 milk/infant-serum study and a 2024 postpartum-depression review. This was **not a systematic review**, and several returned records had no abstract or did not establish a lactation-specific population. Titles and search counts are not outcome evidence. [PubMed search](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

### FAERS limitation

The retrieved FAERS query listed reporting volumes for reactions such as nausea, fatigue, headache, anxiety, diarrhea, dizziness, and depression. These are spontaneous-report counts, not incidence rates or proof of causation. The query was not infant-specific and cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [FAERS query](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) · [FAERS methodology](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist

- Does this evidence apply to my exact product, formulation, and all active ingredients?
- How closely do these studies match my infant’s age, breastfeeding extent, gestational age, and prematurity status?
- Which findings are measured milk or infant-serum concentrations, and which are actual clinical outcomes?
- How should the reported single preterm-infant case be interpreted in relation to my infant’s circumstances?
- What uncertainties or missing evidence should be considered before making a treatment decision?
- What follow-up plan is appropriate for both my health and the infant’s health?
- Could other medicines, supplements, or the underlying maternal condition affect interpretation of symptoms or milk production?

The tool’s continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing treatment can also carry risks and belongs in a discussion with the prescribing clinician. I have not provided a medication decision or dose.

## Evidence brief: sertraline during lactation

**Identity:** The lookup matched the ingredient **sertraline** exactly (RxNorm 36437). The evidence concerns sertraline as a single ingredient; combination-product safety and interactions were not assessed. [S16](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed reports a small observation in which six patients reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; doses were not reported. This is an observation, not proof that sertraline caused the change. [S19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A small mixed-SSRI study reported delayed onset of milk secretory activation among SRI-treated mothers, but no statistically significant difference in feeding difficulties after day 4. Sertraline-specific results were limited because only one participant in that study was taking sertraline. [S19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed product is **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**. Its lactation section states that published data show low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk and that it found no data on effects on milk production. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- The retrieved adult label extract included an adverse-reactions section, but warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug-interactions sections were missing in the returned extraction. Missing sections are a limitation of this lookup, not evidence that those warnings do not exist elsewhere in the full labeling. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Measured infant exposure

- LactMed reports that sertraline is often not detected in infant serum, while norsertraline may be detectable at low levels. [S19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In the returned PubMed abstract for a study of **12 lactating women and 11 mother–infant pairs**—a human milk/infant-serum pharmacokinetic study—sertraline was detected in three nursing infants and norsertraline in six. The abstract also states that detected infant serum concentrations were below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)
- The DailyMed label describes a pooled analysis of **53 mother–infant pairs** in which exclusively human-milk-fed infants had lower serum concentrations than their mothers; the label reports an average infant-to-mother serum-level ratio of 2%, with a reported range of 0%–15%. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

These are research measurements of exposure, not dosing instructions or individualized exposure estimates.

### Observed infant outcomes

- In small observational samples summarized by LactMed, some infants had no observed acute adverse reactions, and one group had reported normal six-month weight gain. These findings are limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous study designs, and incomplete population details. [S19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed describes a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks’ gestation** whose mother used sertraline during pregnancy and postpartum. The infant developed hyperthermia, abnormal muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying. The source reports elevated infant serum concentrations and describes the reaction as probably caused by sertraline in the context of prematurity and reduced metabolism. This is a single case report and should not be generalized to all breastfed infants. [S19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A separate report described sedation in an infant whose mother was taking sertraline along with other medicines, so attribution to sertraline alone is not established. [S19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The retrieved LactMed exposure and infant-outcome sections were truncated. Some chronology and outcomes are therefore missing from this extract; no conclusion should be drawn from the omitted material.

### Literature and evidence limitations

- The PubMed search returned 129 records, but only a bounded relevance subset and abstracts were retrieved. It was not a systematic review, and several records did not establish a lactation-specific population. [S8](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- The returned evidence-base metadata did not establish a study count; missing study counts are unknown, not zero. Reference counts are not study counts. [S19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Source populations vary. The PubMed milk/infant-serum study has mixed returned population labels—pregnancy, lactation, and neonate—while some other records have population fields missing in the returned metadata. Findings should not be generalized beyond the reported populations. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)
- The DailyMed record represents one selected product label, not every sertraline formulation, and its pregnancy section was truncated. The label effective date was November 5, 2026; this is a source-document date, not a guarantee that it is the latest approved labeling. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- FAERS results were not lactation- or infant-specific. They are reporting volume, not incidence or causation, and cannot establish risk for all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S10](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist

- Does this evidence apply to my exact product, formulation, and all active ingredients?
- How closely do these studies match my infant’s age, breastfeeding extent, gestational age, and prematurity status?
- Which findings are measured milk or infant-serum concentrations, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
- How should the single preterm-infant case be interpreted in relation to my infant’s circumstances?
- What uncertainties and missing evidence are most relevant to my situation?
- What follow-up approach should be discussed for both my health and the infant’s health?

The lookup also notes that stopping or changing treatment can carry risks and belongs in a discussion with the prescribing clinician.
